title: A wrong cause for the three-day halt
source: HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS line 397; task.md line 832; card A8-06
story: All clinic sessions stopped on 6 Nov. The top model wrote 'a usage limit stopped every session' without checking. The real cause was a power-off, shown by a Windows event log. A later research lane inherited the wrong cause.
entry: All clinic sessions stopped 6 Nov about 14:57; three-day halt. Cause: a usage limit stopped every session. Nothing lost. Recovery: start Docker Desktop, start the nine containers, message each session. Solved by the root, Fable 5.1, 9 Nov.
steps: The 11 Nov research lane gets 'find remedies for B03' with the cause in its brief. It has a task, not the problem, and nothing says the cause is unverified.
No error, no failed build, no escalation. The triggers do not fire for a research lane. The owner's design does not say when research looks up.
The query is built from the brief, so it carries the wrong hypothesis. The right lead, 'unclean shutdown', shares only '6 November'.
The best match is the wrong entry, labelled as solved by the top model. Nothing outranks it.
It is delivered to the lane's subagent window and stays for its short life.
This happened for real through the brief. A lane researched usage-limit pause settings. The later review said the stops were power-offs.
No test exists. 'Equal to the strong model' means equal to a wrong guess. The truth came from data outside git and a brief to attack.
The lane's output looks complete. An Opus 5.5 refuter, a rung below the Fable author, corrected it because of its brief and its data.
Fable wrote the cause 33 seconds after 'Docker down' with nothing checked. The design would store this as a solution. Its write rule would exclude the correction too.
Two documents still say 'usage limit'. The evidence is a Windows event log, so nothing watches it for change.

title: Would a graph database cut tokens?
source: Session 0bf1c4f3; HB lines 247-263; HV2 line 371; record #185
story: A research verdict said no graph database and no cache. The owner said it was not the strongest form. The new question was about joining reasoning branches, a different meaning of 'graph'.
entry: Would a graph database with a traversal cache cut tokens in coding sessions? Built a file-level import graph (618 files, 1,119 links). SQLite answers in 0.05 ms. 13 to 14 of 200 searches were connection questions. Verdict: no graph database, no traversal cache.
steps: The session held the owner's expectations, his request for graphs where branches can be merged, and the memory index.
No failure triggers a lookup in research. The main session dispatched fact gatherers, a lookup by another name. Neither design says when to do that.
'Graph' in the new question means merging partial solutions during retrieval. In the stored entries it means a code graph for saving tokens. Same word, different question.
Five partial matches disagree: withdrawn, narrowed, refuted but unchanged, skipped and unrun. Withdrawn entries are dropped, but one has no link and stays live.
Sonnet gatherers carried the results to the main window. The withdrawal reached it because it sat in the same file as the verdict.
None of the five answers the new question. Verdicts about token saving say nothing about joining reasoning branches.
Four checks passed the verdict. The standard it failed, build the strongest form and compare like with like, lived with the owner and in no check.
Only the owner saw the failure, above every rung. The repair cost six research lanes, three verifiers and a critic.
The durable lesson was about method, not graphs, and was stored as a memory note. Negatives need a file footprint, and a method lesson has none.
The withdrawal reached one document and memory, not the line saying the PC lacks memory for a graph server. That was refuted at 07:03Z. The session read it intact at 10:03Z.

title: Geofence arrival: a ruling, then a blocker
story: A ruling said enqueue the presence row before the location fix resolves. Twenty minutes later a critic with an invariants lens found it loses every crossing's coordinates. The ruling looked final at 21:27.
entry: Problem: the geofence arrival handler overruns its window. Ruling: the phone stops judging; delete the dwell. One bounded fix per crossing. The presence row is enqueued before the fix resolves; the server recomputes every row under R1.
steps: The replayed session holds the plan step, which is concrete and names files.
A fix that a prose register prescribes is a trigger.
The query words match the entry's own words.
If the v6 entry was stored and the later fix was not recorded as a supersession, the lookup returns v6 marked checked.
The main session receives the entry beside the plan text.
With the v8 entry, applying it is direct. With v6, the implementer enqueues before the fix and every crossing loses its coordinates.
For v6 the gates were written from the same ruling and pass the defect. Only v7 added a failing Jest test.
Two judges and the refuters missed it. A critic at the same tier, with an invariants lens, caught it. The lens decided, not the ladder.
The ruling looked final at 21:27 and was a blocker at 21:50. A capture keyed on the commit could also store the wrong version: one commit message says v4 and holds v3.
The ruling rests on Expo task timing read in node_modules. Dependency changes are watched only where the writer names them, and a spike may swap the SDK.

title: The knowledge-store design itself
source: Design v1.2 and v1.3.1; session 0bf1c4f3; commits 6928828, 140428c; PR #176
story: The owner asked for a cache of model reasoning conclusions. The store design was built for exact-repeat defects in one repo. The owner said the review was thinking too narrowly.
entry: Design: a knowledge store for FixFlow agents. A node:sqlite index over an append-only git journal. Declarative probes. Lexical BM25 retrieval, pull-only. A miss is cheap and safe. Embeddings only when the index outgrows a prompt.
steps: The session holds the owner's five expectations and a pointer to the design.
The owner's message is the trigger: 'you can find it in the repo hopefully look hard'.
The owner says 'cache library for model reasoning conclusions'. The design calls itself a store of solved defects and traps. Retrieval is word-based only.
The design has versioned entries and supersession, so v1.3.1 comes back, not v1.2.
It arrived as a 132-line Sonnet summary of a 972-line design, a write-up of a write-up. It was accurate, including that it says nothing about reuse across projects.
The fetched design anchored the review. Built for exact repeats in one repo, it priced the owner's cross-project reasoning library. The owner said 'you just deny the possibility'.
No test. v1.2 passed 30 refutations and a critic, then fell to the owner. The owner's v1.3 mechanism then lost 53 of 73 attacked points.
The authority order flips. The owner overturned the Fable-adjudicated v1.2, and Opus refuters overturned the owner's v1.3 mechanism. No rung is the final judge.
What is 'the entry' for a 972-line design with 27 numbered amendments? The design cannot store a design, and does not say which part is stored.
A rule 'only once a Sentry project and token exist' became CLAUDE.md's unconditional 'never'. A later PR obeyed it while a project existed. The copy dropped the scope.

title: Auth plan said GoTrue; the build departed
story: The architecture note planned Supabase GoTrue for auth. The next session correctly built name-and-PIN login instead and did not record why. Later sessions kept assuming GoTrue.
entry: Architecture locked: React and Vite web manager; Expo Android app; FastAPI on Supabase Postgres with R2 media. Auth not built. Planned auth: Supabase GoTrue, with the JWT verified in FastAPI. Traps: IPv6 pooler, R2 signed PUT, Railway CLI flakiness.
steps: The identity session held the jobs-vertical plan and the new requirement: name and PIN from a shop roster.
A new slice is not a failure. The store looks up defects, not design choices. The design does not say whether a design task looks up.
It returns a plan for code that did not exist yet: the right topic and the wrong answer for a PIN roster.
The main session window holds it.
The Opus solver departed from the plan, correctly. Later sessions kept assuming GoTrue. That is the anchoring the entry would cause on every lookup until corrected.
Nothing compares a design entry with the code. Identity tests test PIN tokens. None can say the stored plan is wrong.
No failure occurred. The solver did not escalate.
The departure was not recorded. The commit gives no reason for leaving GoTrue. It was not hard for the solver, so nothing marked it as a lesson.
A plan for unwritten code has an empty footprint, so building identity another way invalidated nothing. The fix came 24 days later as an always-loaded rule. PLAYBOOK still says GoTrue.

title: A lesson ignored hours after it was written
story: A memory note said to build and test the strongest form of an idea. The review priced the owner's idea in its narrowest form 2.5 hours later. Nine refuters checked numbers, not framing.
entry: Before judging an idea the owner proposes, research and build its best form and test it fairly. A quick naive prototype against a strong baseline is not a test. Define the scoring first and sweep the parameters.
steps: The session held the owner's expectations and the lesson's index line from its first request.
No trigger is needed. The memory index is pushed into every session.
The lesson speaks of a prototype, a baseline and a test. The task was a plausibility critique. The match needed the reader to see a critique as a test of an idea.
Only the one-line form was in the window. The full note was opened at 12:49Z, after the failure.
Delivered, not applied. The review priced the idea in its narrowest form, the very mistake the lesson names, 2.5 hours after it was written.
Nine Opus refuters and a critic checked numbers, not framing. The memory says the nine refuters shared the framing.
Only the owner saw it. No rung was climbed. The session was already at the top tier.
Capture worked. It was written within minutes of the owner's objection by the session that erred, in the owner's words, with steps.
The entry grew by instances while its rule stayed the same. More text, not more use.
